⏺ The History of Lighthouses

  Lighthouses stand as enduring monuments to humanity's struggle against the sea, their rotating beams cutting through darkness to guide sailors safely to
  shore. Yet the story of these structures extends far deeper into history than most people realize, encompassing thousands of years of technological
  innovation, engineering achievement, and maritime necessity. From ancient signal fires on clifftops to sophisticated automated systems operated by remote
  control, lighthouses represent an evolution not just in construction techniques, but in humanity's fundamental relationship with the ocean and our
  determination to make seafaring safer.

  The earliest lighthouses were not the tall stone towers we imagine today, but rather simple fires burned on high ground to warn ships of hazards. The ancient
  Egyptians maintained beacon fires along the Nile River and Mediterranean coast as early as 1500 BCE, using these flames to guide trading vessels. These early
  light sources were crude by modern standards, fueled by wood or rushes, visible only on clear nights and within limited distances. Yet they represented a
  profound shift in thinking: the recognition that human intervention could improve maritime safety through the strategic placement of light and heat. The
  ancient Greeks and Phoenicians similarly maintained beacon fires along their coastlines, creating informal networks of guidance that became increasingly
  important as maritime trade expanded.

  One of the most famous ancient lighthouses was the Pharos of Alexandria, constructed around 280 BCE on the island of Pharos near Alexandria, Egypt. Standing
  between 330 and 450 feet tall depending on historical account, the Pharos was one of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World and served as a model for
  lighthouse design for centuries. Built during the reign of Ptolemy II, this structure utilized mirrors or polished bronze to reflect sunlight during the day
